Wounded
wōōnd´ĕd
adj. (pierced, hurt, injured; rendering Hebrew chalal, nakah, Greek traumatizō)
From Saxon wund, a hurt. Isaiah 53 makes the word the hinge of substitution: He wounded, and by His stripes we healed.

Biblical Definition

Wounded in Scripture is the language of substitution and of the soul's deepest injury. Isaiah states the exchange in one verse: “he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities: the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed” (Isa 53:5) — four clauses, and in each the wound is His and the benefit is ours. Zechariah adds a strange and haunting detail of the smitten Shepherd: “What are these wounds in thine hands? Then he shall answer, Those with which I was wounded in the house of my friends” (Zec 13:6). Proverbs then names the injury no medicine reaches: “The spirit of a man will sustain his infirmity; but a wounded spirit who can bear?” (Pro 18:14) — a man's inner strength carries his bodily weakness, but when the inner man himself is wounded there is nothing left underneath to do the carrying. The answer to that question is the first verse: the only cure for a wounded spirit is a wounded Saviour, and the stripes that heal are His.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines wound as a breach of the skin and flesh of an animal, or of the bark of a plant, caused by violence; and figuratively an injury to reputation or to the feelings.

expand to see more

WOUND, n. A breach of the skin and flesh of an animal, or of the bark and wood of a tree, or of the bark and substance of other plants, caused by violence or external force.

2. Injury; hurt; as a wound given to credit or reputation.

WOUND, v.t. To hurt by violence; as, to wound the head or the arm.

2. To hurt the feelings; to pain.

Key Scripture

Isa 53:5 — "But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities: the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed."

Zec 13:6 — "And one shall say unto him, What are these wounds in thine hands? Then he shall answer, Those with which I was wounded in the house of my friends."

Pro 18:14 — "The spirit of a man will sustain his infirmity; but a wounded spirit who can bear?"

Psa 147:3 — "He healeth the broken in heart, and bindeth up their wounds."

Modern Corruption

The wounded spirit has been transferred wholesale to the clinic, and the church has largely accepted the transfer — ceding a category Scripture treats as spiritual and answers with a wounded Christ.

expand to see more

Proverbs 18:14 asks a question the modern age answers almost entirely in one register: a wounded spirit is a condition to be assessed, named, and managed, and the pastor's role shrinks to referral. Some of that referral is right — bodies affect souls, and Scripture never despises ordinary means or the physician. But a church that has no category of its own for a wounded spirit has surrendered the very thing it exists to address, and it will have nothing to say when the assessment is complete and the man is still in the dark.

Scripture's answer is not a technique but a Person with wounds. Isaiah 53 does not merely sympathise with the injured; it says the injury was transferred — wounded for our transgressions, and with his stripes we are healed. Zechariah's detail is that the wounds were received in the house of His friends, which means He is not a stranger to being hurt by those closest to Him. The psalmist puts it plainly: He healeth the broken in heart, and bindeth up their wounds. Binding up is slow, deliberate work, and He is described as doing it Himself.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew chalal (H2490), to pierce or wound fatally, and nakah (H5221), to smite; Greek traumatizō (G5135), to wound — the pierced Servant and the pierced spirit.

expand to see more

Hebrew chalal (H2490) — to pierce, wound, profane; “he was wounded for our transgressions” (Isa 53:5).

Hebrew nakah (H5221) — to strike, smite, wound; the smitten Shepherd of Zec 13:7.

Hebrew nakeh (H5218) with ruach — a stricken or wounded spirit (Pro 18:14), the injury that leaves nothing underneath to carry the man.

Usage

"“He was wounded for our transgressions” — the wound His, the healing ours."

"“Those with which I was wounded in the house of my friends” — hurt by the nearest."

"“A wounded spirit who can bear?” — the question only a wounded Saviour answers."
